The model aims to capture a comprehensive representation of the world by integrating spatial, temporal, and acoustic information, enabling it to perceive, predict, and act across physical and digital environments.

FLUX 3 supports diverse capabilities including text-to-video generation with audio up to 20 seconds, image-to-video generation, video-to-video transformation, and multilingual dialogue. Early evaluations show FLUX 3 outperforming several existing models in video generation quality and style diversity. The model is currently available in Early Access, with ongoing development expected to improve its performance further.

items.title: Black Forest Labs and mimic launch FLUX-mimic, a next-generation video-action model for robot manipulation based on the multimodal FLUX 3 foundation model [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Flux 3 X Mimic: The Next Generation of Video-Action Models
items.summary:
Black Forest Labs (BFL) and mimic have developed FLUX-mimic, a video-action model built on the FLUX 3 multimodal foundation model that jointly generates images, video, audio, and robot actions. FLUX 3 was trained to understand physical world dynamics through video prediction, enabling it to model cause and effect, motion, and contact, which supports both content creation and robotic manipulation.

FLUX-mimic integrates BFL's visual foundation model expertise with mimic's robotics and deployment capabilities, resulting in a model tested and deployed on real production lines, including at Audi. The model's single backbone architecture allows it to predict robot actions without sacrificing video generation quality, demonstrating that physical AI and content creation can share a unified underlying model of the world.

items.summary:
A developer critiques elaborate workflows for AI-assisted code writing, stating that excessive constraints in prompts narrow the model's effectiveness and lead to subpar results. They suggest a simpler two-step approach where the AI is first given relevant context and then instructed on what to build, allowing the model to naturally follow conventions and patterns without micromanagement.

The article highlights that developers often resist fully trusting AI because it challenges their traditional sense of control and value tied to coding output. Instead of adding complex layers of oversight, the author encourages embracing AI's capabilities and focusing on higher-level tasks like choosing the technology stack and monitoring AI output quality, while avoiding unnecessary procedural overhead.

items.originalTitle: Silicon Valley Is Completely Divided Over Chinese AI
items.summary:
Silicon Valley is deeply divided over the rise of Chinese open-weight AI models, with major AI companies like Anthropic raising alarms about intellectual property theft and security risks, while smaller startups oppose US government restrictions. The debate centers on the rapid spread of these models, which lack the safety guardrails of proprietary systems but enable faster innovation and broader access.

Anthropic has accused Chinese firms Alibaba and Moonshot AI of illicitly using its technology through distillation attacks, prompting concerns in Washington and the Valley. Meanwhile, a coalition of over 200 startups, including YCombinator, has lobbied against banning open-weight models, arguing that such restrictions would stifle competition and favor large AI giants. Investors like Bill Gurley emphasize the importance of open models for startup growth, while critics warn of potential security vulnerabilities.

The controversy highlights a tension between protecting proprietary AI advancements and fostering an open ecosystem that benefits smaller players and innovation. US policymakers face challenges balancing national security, economic interests, and the future of AI development amid this complex landscape.

The initiative is described by the White House as comparable in urgency to the Manhattan Project and aims to accelerate scientific discovery by leveraging artificial intelligence.

It also signals a move toward prioritizing individual researchers and private companies over traditional academic institutions, with political appointees gaining more control over federal funding decisions. Critics warn this approach treats science like a startup, potentially undermining the slow, uncertain nature of basic research that has historically driven major discoveries.

Shares of Google parent Alphabet fell 7% on Thursday after the company disclosed a further increase in capital expenditures this year—money it will spend on new AI chips, servers and data centers. The drop all but wiped out the gains the stock had enjoyed so far this year.

But Alphabet was among the worst hit, along with Tesla, which also reported sharply higher capex on Wednesday and whose shares fell 15% on Thursday. It’s tough to consider Tesla’s stock valuation on any kind of rational basis, given that it trades based more on its connection to Elon Musk than reality. But Alphabet is a different animal.

items.originalTitle: The Startups Angling to Go Public After Anthropic
items.summary:
Before we get into today’s column, some breaking news: Stripe is in talks to buy OpenRouter for about $10 billion. The news follows our report Friday that the $1.3 billion-valuation startup, which helps companies choose the best and cheapest AI models, was the target of takeover interest. Databricks was also in early discussions to buy the startup, we reported today. For more on why Stripe can make big acquisitions, read our exclusive reporting on its financials here. 

Mutual funds and other large investors considering buying into Anthropic’s initial public offering are slated to meet with the AI company over the next several days. Along with Anthropic’s plans to secure compute and the rise of Chinese models, big investors are likely to have questions about the structure of the IPO—including when shareholders can sell. 

The potential for Anthropic to dump the typical IPO playbook was raised in a scoop by Cory earlier today. Anthropic is considering requiring rank-and-file employees—rather than just top executives—to sell stock through rigid trading schedules. 

It’s not just the investors who will be closely following Anthropic’s IPO moves. Startups are keeping an eye on the listing, which could happen as soon as September, as they consider their own public plans. No one wants to compete with Anthropic for investors’ attention. But if it goes well, it could unlock a wave of IPOs from other tech startups, particularly those riding the groundswell of consumer and business interest in AI—as well as others that argue they’re immune from AI-generated volatility.

items.summary:
In 2020, 22-year-old Aakash Thumaty was a product manager at Salesforce when he wrote an essay, “Value Driven Innovation at Shopify and the Incumbency Trap at Salesforce,” which argued against Salesforce’s subscription-based business model. He sent it to Bret Taylor, who at the time was Salesforce’s chief operating officer. To Thumaty’s surprise, Taylor shared it with other executives at the company.

Six years later, Thumaty and Taylor’s paths are crossing again. Sierra, the AI customer support startup Taylor now leads, is acquiring Thumaty’s three-person startup, Takeoff, which develops agents that can work on tasks for long periods of time, the companies told The Information exclusively.

They wouldn’t disclose details but it’s unlikely to have been a high priced acquisition. items.summary:
As Anthropic prepares to go public, it is considering a highly unusual move to require rank-and-file employees to sell stock through rigid trading schedules so they don’t run afoul of insider trading laws, said a person familiar with the matter and a person briefed on it.

At companies that have used such trading plans, typically only top executives and some finance and legal staff adopt them. The arrangements, called 10b5-1 plans, require executives and directors to sell stock according to preset schedules that outline how many shares they’ll sell and at what prices.
